expect.statement: Whether amphetamine use (amphetamine or methamphetamine) is associated with violence after accounting for other factors is not settled. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the pooled adjusted odds ratio was 1.4 (95% CI 0.8–2.4; 6 studies), against 2.2 (1.2–4.1; 10 studies, I² 95%) unadjusted. In unadjusted post hoc subgroups, violent behaviour (hostility rating scales, violent behaviour or sexual exploitation reported in surveys, and violent or self-destructive behaviour in an emergency department) was associated (3.7, 3.1–4.5) and violent offending was not clearly associated (1.0, 0.4–2.7; I² 94%). For amphetamine use disorder the review has a single study: among offenders whose punishment was reduced or waived because of mental disorder, those with the disorder had more violent re-offending over 7 years (unadjusted OR 6.2, 3.1–12.3; 52 people with the disorder; quality score 43%). The violence studies had among the lowest quality ratings in the review, with poor measurement of use; the review's authors judge that large effects in two population surveys and two longitudinal studies suggest that an association may exist but needs confirmation. The review also describes a within-person analysis of the same Australian treatment cohort as the psychosis study in section 9, in which severe hostility was more frequent during periods of use after adjustment for concurrent other drug use; that paper has not yet been read. A later general-population birth cohort, not in the review (Christchurch, New Zealand; about 1,000 people interviewed at 21, 25, 30 and 35; 28% used methamphetamine or amphetamine at least once between 18 and 35), found that use in a period went with more self-reported violence in the same period after adjustment for childhood and adolescent factors and for concurrent depression, anxiety, alcohol and cannabis use disorders, life stress, unemployment and psychotic symptoms: perpetration OR 1.60 (1.01–2.54), victimisation 1.57 (1.00–2.47), intimate-partner violence perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30) and victimisation 1.09 (0.80–1.49). Odds were higher among the 51 people who had used at least weekly (perpetration 4.84, 2.48–9.46), in an analysis adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only that related the heaviest use in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35, so the two need not fall in the same period; less frequent use was not clearly associated with perpetration (1.13 and 1.40, intervals including 1). Use and violence were reported for the same periods, so which came first is unknown, and other illicit drug use was not adjusted for.
expect.plain: Is amphetamine use, including meth, linked to violence once other factors are taken into account? The evidence doesn't settle it. In a review of mostly weak studies, the link seen in raw numbers shrank and became uncertain after adjustment; in the raw numbers it was seen for violent behaviour but not clearly for violent offences. A later study followed about 1,000 people in New Zealand from age 18 to 35. In periods when they used meth or speed, people were somewhat more likely to report attacking someone or being attacked, even after many other factors were taken into account. The few who had used at least weekly had higher odds, in an analysis that took fewer factors into account. But use and violence were reported for the same years, so the study cannot show which came first, and it did not take other illegal drugs into account. One study that compared people with themselves found more hostility in periods of use; it has not been read yet. The review's authors think a link may exist but needs to be confirmed.
expect.magnitude: Review (any use): adjusted OR 1.4 (0.8–2.4), 6 studies, I² 25%; unadjusted 2.2 (1.2–4.1), 10 studies, I² 95%; violent behaviour 3.7 (3.1–4.5); violent offending 1.0 (0.4–2.7). Birth cohort (any use in a period, fully adjusted): perpetration 1.60 (1.01–2.54), victimisation 1.57 (1.00–2.47), intimate-partner perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30), intimate-partner victimisation 1.09 (0.80–1.49); at least weekly use against never (heaviest use in any period, violence at any time from 18 to 35), adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only: perpetration 4.84 (2.48–9.46), victimisation 3.62 (1.88–6.96).
expect.population: General-population (including a New Zealand birth cohort followed from 18 to 35), clinical and justice samples
expect.exposure: Any amphetamine use (in the birth cohort, self-reported use of methamphetamine or amphetamine in each interview period)
expect.outcome: Violent behaviour or violent offending (in the birth cohort, self-reported perpetration and victimisation, including intimate-partner violence)
expect.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The review's violence studies had among the lowest quality scores (56–58%), with poor measurement of use. The birth cohort is stronger but at high risk of bias overall on its study card (ROBINS-E): use and violence reported for the same periods (reverse causation possible), self-reported and uncorroborated outcomes, and no adjustment for other illicit drug use, with fully adjusted estimates at the margin of no association.
expect.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the adjusted estimates of the review and of the cohort are similar (1.4 against 1.55–1.60 for perpetration, victimisation and intimate-partner perpetration); the high heterogeneity of the review's unadjusted pools is partly explained by the post hoc split between violent behaviour and violent offending.
expect.grade.domains.imprecision.note: The review's adjusted interval includes no association (0.8–2.4), and the cohort's fully adjusted lower limits are 1.00–1.04.
expect.grade.domains.dose_response.note: Considered and not applied: the cohort's gradient comes from an analysis adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only, which relates the heaviest use in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35, rests on 51 people who used at least weekly, is concentrated in that top category for perpetration, and could be produced by confounding that grows with frequency of use (other drug use, involvement in drug markets), which runs away from the null; the within-person dose-related finding in the treatment cohort (McKetin et al., 2014) has not been read.
expect.grade.reasoning: Observational: mostly cross-sectional studies in the review, plus one prospective birth cohort; starts low. Risk of bias −1: the review's violence studies had among the lowest quality scores (56–58%), with poor measurement of use, and the cohort is at high risk of bias on ROBINS-E (same-period measurement, self-report, no adjustment for other illicit drugs). Imprecision −1: the pooled adjusted interval includes no association (0.8–2.4), and the cohort's fully adjusted lower limits are 1.00–1.04. Not upgraded for dose-response (see the domain note). Certainty very low. Status mixed: in the review's unadjusted data, violent behaviour and violent offending point different ways (3.7 against 1.0, with I² 94% left unexplained within offending), while the adjusted estimates of the review and the birth cohort agree in direction; inconsistency is not rated down because the rating rests on the adjusted estimates. Relation kept as insufficient evidence: the cohort's estimates agree with the review's adjusted point estimate and point to a modest association, but the review's adjusted interval includes no association, the cohort's fully adjusted lower limits sit at 1.00–1.04 in one cohort at high risk of bias with same-period reporting, and neither source can show that use came before violence. The cohort shares authors with the review (Foulds, McKetin), although its data are not in the pooled estimates. On the reading list: the within-person analysis of the MATES cohort (McKetin et al., 2014), which sits inside the pooled estimate; a systematic review of drug-administration studies of aggression (O'Malley et al., 2022, DOI list item 110); and McKetin et al. (2020), on methamphetamine use and crime in Australian longitudinal data, which shares three authors with the birth-cohort paper (McKetin, Boden, Foulds). When read, McKetin et al. (2020) would sit beside the birth cohort as a second longitudinal source, on violent crime; whether shared authors or data make it replication by the same team must be checked before it counts as independent.

set.statement: After accounting for other factors, amphetamine use (amphetamine or methamphetamine) is associated with more violence in two longitudinal studies by overlapping research groups, one in the general population and one in people dependent on methamphetamine; a meta-analysis of mostly cross-sectional studies found an adjusted association in the same direction that was not statistically clear, and none of these sources can show that use came before the violence, so whether use causes violence is not settled. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the pooled adjusted odds ratio was 1.4 (95% CI 0.8–2.4; 6 studies), against 2.2 (1.2–4.1; 10 studies, I² 95%) unadjusted. In unadjusted post hoc subgroups, violent behaviour (hostility rating scales, violent behaviour or sexual exploitation reported in surveys, and violent or self-destructive behaviour in an emergency department) was associated (3.7, 3.1–4.5) and violent offending was not clearly associated (1.0, 0.4–2.7; I² 94%). For amphetamine use disorder the review has a single study: among offenders whose punishment was reduced or waived because of mental disorder, those with the disorder had more violent re-offending over 7 years (unadjusted OR 6.2, 3.1–12.3; 52 people with the disorder; quality score 43%). The violence studies had among the lowest quality ratings in the review, with poor measurement of use; the review's authors judge that large effects in two population surveys and two longitudinal studies suggest that an association may exist but needs confirmation. The review also describes a within-person analysis of the same Australian treatment cohort as the psychosis study in section 9, in which severe hostility was more frequent during periods of use after adjustment for concurrent other drug use; that paper has not yet been read. A later general-population birth cohort, not in the review (Christchurch, New Zealand; about 1,000 people interviewed at 21, 25, 30 and 35; 28% used methamphetamine or amphetamine at least once between 18 and 35), found that use in a period went with more self-reported violence in the same period after adjustment for childhood and adolescent factors and for concurrent depression, anxiety, alcohol and cannabis use disorders, life stress, unemployment and psychotic symptoms: perpetration OR 1.60 (1.01–2.54), victimisation 1.57 (1.00–2.47), intimate-partner violence perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30) and victimisation 1.09 (0.80–1.49). Odds were higher among the 51 people who had used at least weekly (perpetration 4.84, 2.48–9.46), in an analysis adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only that related the heaviest use in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35, so the two need not fall in the same period; less frequent use was not clearly associated with perpetration (1.13 and 1.40, intervals including 1). Use and violence were reported for the same periods, so which came first is unknown, and other illicit drug use was not adjusted for. A second longitudinal study, also later than the review, followed 469 people dependent on methamphetamine in Sydney and Brisbane (mostly people entering treatment, most of whom injected; the same cohort as the hostility analysis inside the review), with reports for the past month at entry, 3 months, 1 year and 3 years (2006–2010). Self-reported crime involving violence, such as violence in a robbery or assault, was reported in 113 of 927 months with methamphetamine use (12%) and 19 of 593 months without (3%). Comparing each person's months with and without use, which removes the influence of stable personal characteristics, the odds were 8.2 times higher (4.2–15.9) unadjusted and 3.4 times higher (1.5–8.0) after adjustment for age, income, unemployment, unstable housing and concurrent alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use; unadjusted percentages rose with days of use, and the adjusted dose estimates are only in a supplement that has not been read. Use and crime were reported for the same month in the same interview, treatment and imprisonment during follow-up were not taken into account, and the analysis was exploratory; the authors say that their intervals are wide because few participants committed crime in months without use, and that the results apply to people dependent on methamphetamine, not to recreational use. The two longitudinal studies share three authors (McKetin, Boden, Foulds), and the second shares four with the review (McKetin, Foulds, Degenhardt, Farrell), so their agreement is not independent replication.
set.plain: Is amphetamine use, including meth, linked to violence once other factors are taken into account? Two long-term studies found a link even after other factors were taken into account, but neither can show that meth causes violence, and the two studies share authors. A review of mostly weak studies found that the link seen in raw numbers shrank and became uncertain after adjustment; in the raw numbers it was seen for violent behaviour but not clearly for violent offences. A study in New Zealand followed about 1,000 people from age 18 to 35. In periods when they used meth or speed, people were somewhat more likely to report attacking someone or being attacked, even after many other factors were taken into account. The few who had used at least weekly had higher odds, in an analysis that took fewer factors into account. A study in Australia followed 469 people dependent on meth for up to three years and compared each person's months of use with their own months without. Violent crime was reported in 12 of 100 months with meth use and 3 of 100 months without, and the link remained after age, money problems and other drug use were taken into account. But in both studies people reported use and violence for the same periods, so the studies cannot show which came first, and the Australian study did not take treatment or time in prison into account. One study that compared people with themselves found more hostility in periods of use; it has not been read yet. The review's authors think a link may exist but needs to be confirmed.
set.magnitude: Review (any use): adjusted OR 1.4 (0.8–2.4), 6 studies, I² 25%; unadjusted 2.2 (1.2–4.1), 10 studies, I² 95%; violent behaviour 3.7 (3.1–4.5); violent offending 1.0 (0.4–2.7). Birth cohort (any use in a period, fully adjusted): perpetration 1.60 (1.01–2.54), victimisation 1.57 (1.00–2.47), intimate-partner perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30), intimate-partner victimisation 1.09 (0.80–1.49); at least weekly use against never (heaviest use in any period, violence at any time from 18 to 35), adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only: perpetration 4.84 (2.48–9.46), victimisation 3.62 (1.88–6.96). Dependent cohort (within-person, months with any methamphetamine use against the same people's months without; self-reported violent crime in the past month): 12% against 3% of months (113 of 927 against 19 of 593); odds ratio 8.2 (4.2–15.9) unadjusted, 5.3 (2.6–10.7) adjusted for age and socio-economic factors, 3.4 (1.5–8.0) also adjusted for other drug use.
set.population: General-population (a New Zealand birth cohort followed from 18 to 35), clinical and justice samples, including an Australian cohort of people dependent on methamphetamine
set.exposure: Any amphetamine use (in the birth cohort, self-reported use of methamphetamine or amphetamine in each interview period; in the dependent cohort, any self-reported methamphetamine use in the past month)
set.comparator: No use (in the dependent cohort, the same people's months without use)
set.outcome: Violent behaviour or violent offending (in the birth cohort, self-reported perpetration and victimisation, including intimate-partner violence; in the dependent cohort, self-reported crime involving violence in the past month)
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The review's violence studies had among the lowest quality scores (56–58%), with poor measurement of use. Both longitudinal studies are at high risk of bias overall on their study cards (ROBINS-E), without a single high domain: use and violence reported for the same periods (reverse causation possible) and by self-report, without corroboration; no adjustment for other illicit drug use in the birth cohort, whose fully adjusted estimates sit at the margin of no association; and, in the dependent cohort, no account of treatment, imprisonment or other changes over time, in an exploratory analysis.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the adjusted estimates agree in direction (review 1.4; birth cohort 1.55–1.60 for perpetration, victimisation and intimate-partner perpetration; dependent cohort 3.4 for violent crime). The larger estimate in the dependent cohort fits its population (people dependent on methamphetamine) and its scale: odds ratios comparing months within the same person are not on the same scale as population-averaged or between-person odds ratios. The high heterogeneity of the review's unadjusted pools is partly explained by the post hoc split between violent behaviour and violent offending.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: The review's adjusted interval includes no association (0.8–2.4), the birth cohort's fully adjusted lower limits are 1.00–1.04, and the dependent cohort's interval is wide (1.5–8.0), resting on 19 months with violent crime among the 593 months without use.
set.grade.domains.dose_response.note: Considered and not applied: the birth cohort's gradient comes from an analysis adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only, which relates the heaviest use in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35, rests on 51 people who used at least weekly, is concentrated in that top category for perpetration, and could be produced by confounding that grows with frequency of use (other drug use, involvement in drug markets), which runs away from the null; in the dependent cohort the article shows the gradient only as unadjusted percentages pooled across people (Fig. 1), and the adjusted dose estimates are in a supplement that has not been read.
set.grade.domains.large_effect.note: Not applied: the dependent cohort's adjusted odds ratio for violent crime (3.4) has a lower limit of 1.5, and the biases that remain (same-month self-report, changes around treatment entry, drug-market involvement) can run away from the null.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational: mostly cross-sectional studies in the review, plus two longitudinal cohorts; starts low. Risk of bias −1: the review's violence studies had among the lowest quality scores (56–58%), with poor measurement of use, and both cohorts are at high risk of bias on ROBINS-E (use and violence self-reported for the same periods; no adjustment for other illicit drugs in the birth cohort; no account of treatment or imprisonment in the dependent cohort). Imprecision −1: the pooled adjusted interval includes no association (0.8–2.4), the birth cohort's fully adjusted lower limits are 1.00–1.04, and the dependent cohort's interval (1.5–8.0) rests on few months with violent crime without use. Not upgraded for dose-response or large effect (see the domain notes). Certainty very low. Relation: is associated with, rather than insufficient evidence, because the adjusted association now appears in two longitudinal cohorts, in a general population and in people dependent on methamphetamine, with intervals that exclude no association, and the review's adjusted pooled estimate points the same way; the very low rating says how uncertain this association is, and whether use causes violence is a separate question that none of the sources can settle, because use and violence were reported for the same periods. Status: replicated by the same team. The adjusted estimates agree in direction, but the two cohorts share three authors (McKetin, Boden, Foulds), the dependent-cohort paper shares four with the review (McKetin, Foulds, Degenhardt, Farrell), and the dependent cohort is the same sample as the within-person hostility analysis inside the review's pooled estimate (McKetin et al., 2014, not yet read), so the agreement is not independent replication. In the review's unadjusted data, violent behaviour and violent offending point different ways (3.7 against 1.0, with I² 94% left unexplained within offending); the dependent cohort's within-person result for self-reported violent crime runs against the unadjusted offending estimate but does not explain that heterogeneity. The rating rests on the adjusted estimates, so this is noted rather than rated down. On the reading list: McKetin et al. (2014); a systematic review of drug-administration studies of aggression (O'Malley et al., 2022, DOI list item 110).

evidence_add.locator: Methods › 2.1. Participants and procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and 2.1.1.1. Crime (p. 2); Methods › 2.1.2. Design and statistical analysis, Table 1 (violent crime row and notes) and Results › 3.2. Changes in crime during periods of methamphetamine use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3)
evidence_add.extracted: MATES cohort (Sydney and Brisbane, recruited 2006–2007, followed to 2010): 469 people with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence at entry (from 400 people entering community treatment and 101 recruited through needle and syringe programmes and outreach), interviewed about the past month at baseline, 3 months (379), 12 months (357) and 3 years (315); 1,518 person-months for violent crime. Violent crime (any crime involving violence, such as violence in a robbery or assault, self-reported on the Opiate Treatment Index crime scale): 19 of 593 months without methamphetamine use (3%) against 113 of 927 months with use (12%). Within-person odds ratios, months with use against months without: unadjusted 8.2 (95% CI 4.2–15.9); adjusted for time-varying age, income, unemployment and unstable accommodation 5.3 (2.6–10.7); also adjusted for alcohol and cannabis (0, 1–15, 16+ days) and any cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use 3.4 (1.5–8.0), p = 0.005.

evidence_add.locator: Methods › 2.1.2. Design and statistical analysis and Results › 3.1. Characteristics of the sample, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Results › 3.2, 3rd paragraph (p. 3, continuing on p. 4) and Fig. 1 (p. 4); Discussion › 4.1. Limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 5)
evidence_add.extracted: The analysis was exploratory and not pre-registered; the methods describe random-effects logistic models with a random intercept and use of the fixed-effects option for the within-person effect, and the number of participants contributing to each estimate is not reported. Use and crime were reported for the same month in the same interview; treatment received and imprisonment during follow-up are not covariates, and tobacco is not among the covariates. Methamphetamine was used in 61% of observed months (median 10 days in months of use; injection the main route in 80%). Crime rose with days of use in unadjusted percentages pooled across months (Fig. 1: no use, 1–15 and 16+ days); the adjusted dose estimates are only in a supplementary table, not available. The authors state that crime was self-reported, not convictions; that the direction of the same-month relationship could be disputed; that few participants committed crime in months without use, giving wide confidence limits, and small numbers limit the dose findings; and that the results apply to people dependent on methamphetamine, most of whom injected, not to recreational use. Editors' reading of Fig. 1 (no values printed): violent crime in about 3%, 9% and 19% of months with no use, 1–15 days and 16+ days of use.

evidence_add.locator: Author list, Abstract (Conclusions) and Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 1); Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 2); Discussion, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (p. 4); reference list (p. 6)
evidence_add.extracted: The authors conclude that use was associated with significant increases in crime beyond premorbid risk and that crime is a likely social consequence of use; in the discussion they call the evidence robust and say that violent crime among people who use methamphetamine is not only a consequence of pre-existing risk, while noting that they cannot tell whether the violence was instrumental (for example robbery) or expressive (for example domestic assault). They state that they applied the same within-person approach earlier to hostility and psychotic symptoms (McKetin et al., 2014 and 2013b). Three of the four authors of the birth-cohort study (Foulds, Boden, McKetin; Foulds et al., 2020) and four authors of the 2019 review (McKetin, Foulds, Degenhardt, Farrell) are authors of this paper.

change: First reader (AI reader 29) from the PDF of McKetin et al. (2020; pp. 1–6), a within-person analysis of the MATES cohort of 469 people dependent on methamphetamine: three anchors added (located; one supports, two qualify). Self-reported violent crime in 12% of months with use against 3% without; within-person odds ratio 8.2 (4.2–15.9) unadjusted and 3.4 (1.5–8.0) after adjustment for age, socio-economic factors and other drug use. Relation insufficient evidence → is associated with, and status mixed → replicated by the same team: the adjusted association now appears in two longitudinal cohorts (a general population and people dependent on methamphetamine) with intervals excluding no association, and the review's adjusted estimate points the same way; the cohorts share three authors, and the MATES sample is also inside the review's pooled estimate through its hostility analysis. Certainty unchanged (very low: risk of bias −1, imprecision −1); dose-response and large effect considered and not applied (adjusted dose estimates only in an unread supplement; remaining biases can run away from the null). The birth-cohort anchor with the fully adjusted estimates now supports rather than qualifies. Statement, plain text, magnitude, population, exposure, comparator, outcome, domain notes and reasoning rewritten; whether use causes violence remains not settled. The reasoning now also names the dependent-cohort paper's author overlap with the review (McKetin, Foulds, Degenhardt, Farrell).

expect.statement: In one study of 50 sibling pairs, in each of which one sibling met DSM-IV criteria for stimulant dependence and the other had no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse (the paper's criterion), both siblings had lower white-matter fractional anisotropy than 50 unrelated controls matched for age and IQ, and shared three grey-matter clusters of difference from them: a larger left amygdala, a larger left putamen, and smaller volume across the left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula. The white-matter, putamen and posterior insula differences were more alike within families than between unrelated people; the amygdala difference was not. The main report names no hippocampal difference (it reports a larger medial temporal lobe, with the left amygdala as the shared cluster), no orbitofrontal or anterior insular difference, and no direct comparison of the two siblings; a review describes a larger hippocampus in both siblings and smaller orbitofrontal and anterior insular volumes in the dependent siblings only, which may come from the paper's supplement, not yet read. Differences shared by the two siblings suggest a familial vulnerability, genetic or from the shared family environment, that may predate drug use; the study cannot show that it does, because nobody was assessed before use began. In the dependent siblings, lower fractional anisotropy and some grey-matter regions went with longer stimulant use (reported in the supplement), which fits an additional effect of use. The main report does not name the stimulants used; according to a review, the dependent participants mostly used cocaine, and whether any used methamphetamine is not reported in the sources read.
expect.plain: Brothers and sisters of people dependent on stimulants, who had no history of long-term drug or alcohol problems themselves, shared some of the same brain differences from unrelated volunteers. That suggests some differences run in families and may come before drug use, although nobody was scanned before they started using. In the dependent person, some differences were larger the longer they had used stimulants, which suggests the drug use may add to them. A review reports other differences found only in the dependent person, but the study's main report does not name or test them. Most of the dependent people in that study used cocaine, according to a review; it is not known whether any used meth.
expect.magnitude: No standardized effect sizes or cluster statistics in the main report. Fractional anisotropy: group difference F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001, which implies 144 of the 150 participants analysed (editors' calculation: η² about 0.27). Within-family similarity (permutation tests, uncorrected for multiple testing): white matter P = 0.004, putamen P = 0.013, posterior insula P = 0.012, amygdala P = 0.144 (not familial).
expect.population: Sibling pairs discordant for stimulant dependence (mostly cocaine)
expect.comparator: Biological siblings with no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse (the paper's criterion); unrelated controls matched for age and IQ
expect.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card (provisional; the supplement was not read): sex, education and other drug use not reported in the main report, smoking more common in both sibling groups and checked only for grey matter, 6 of 150 participants missing from the analyses by the degrees of freedom, and only the clusters shared by both siblings described.
expect.grade.reasoning: One cross-sectional study of 50 sibling pairs, read in full except its supplement. Starts low (observational). Risk of bias, one level: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card (provisional), because sex, education and other drug use are not reported in the main report, smoking was more common in both sibling groups and was checked only for grey matter, the degrees of freedom imply that 6 of 150 participants are missing from the analyses without explanation, and only the clusters shared by both siblings are described. Indirectness, one level: the main report does not name the stimulants, which according to a review were mostly cocaine. Imprecision, one level: 50 people per group, voxel-wise whole-brain tests whose correction is described only in the supplement, and familiality tests without correction for multiple testing (three of the six would not pass a Bonferroni threshold, editors' calculation). Certainty very low. The claim is rated as an association; whether the shared differences predate use cannot be settled by this design.
expect.evidence.0.extracted: 50 sibling pairs, one sibling with DSM-IV stimulant dependence and the other with no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse, against 50 unrelated volunteers matched for age and IQ. Both siblings had lower white-matter fractional anisotropy than the volunteers (tract skeleton, F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001), and it was more alike within true sibling pairs than within random pairs (permutation P = 0.004). Three grey-matter clusters were shared by both sibling groups: a larger left amygdala and left putamen, and a smaller left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula; the putamen (P = 0.013) and posterior insula (P = 0.012) differences were familial by the permutation test, the amygdala difference was not (P = 0.144). The main report names no hippocampal, orbitofrontal or anterior insular difference, reports no direct comparison of the two siblings and does not say which stimulants were used; the supplement, which holds the cluster statistics and the sample characteristics, was not read.

set.statement: In one UK study of 50 pairs of full siblings, in each of which one sibling met DSM-IV-TR criteria for stimulant dependence and the other had no personal history of substance dependence other than nicotine (the supplement's enrolment criterion; the main report says no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse), both siblings had lower white-matter fractional anisotropy than 50 unrelated controls without a personal or family history of dependence, similar in age and verbal IQ, and shared three grey-matter clusters of difference from them: a larger left amygdala, a larger left putamen, and smaller volume across the left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula. The white-matter, putamen and posterior insula differences were more alike within families than in random pairings (one-tailed permutation tests, not corrected for multiple testing); the amygdala difference was not. The imaging analyses included 146 people for grey matter and 145 for white matter; the grey-matter maps were thresholded to allow about one false-positive cluster per map, and the shared clusters are the overlap of two comparisons with the same control group. More of the non-dependent siblings than of the controls smoked (55% against 12%), and the sexes were unbalanced (51% and 64% men); a re-analysis of non-smokers kept the grey-matter differences, but no smoking check is reported for white matter, and neither this nor the single-sex re-analysis gives statistics. Differences shared by the two siblings suggest a familial vulnerability, genetic or from the shared family environment, that may predate drug use; the study cannot show that it does, because nobody was assessed before use began. Neither the main report nor its supplement names an orbitofrontal or anterior insular difference or compares the two siblings directly; a review describes a larger hippocampus in both siblings and smaller orbitofrontal and anterior insular volumes in the dependent siblings only: the hippocampal statement may come from the supplement, which labels the shared medial temporal cluster amygdala/hippocampus in places, but the orbitofrontal and anterior insular statement cannot be traced to the study. The supplement maps regions where lower fractional anisotropy and grey matter went with more years of stimulant use in the dependent siblings, without statistics or region names and without adjustment for age, which rises with years of use, or for their other dependence (55% on opiates, 26% on alcohol), so they do not separate an effect of stimulant use from these. The dependent siblings were still using stimulants when tested (urine positive in all but three); 94% were dependent on cocaine and 6% on amphetamines, and methamphetamine is not mentioned.
set.plain: Brothers and sisters of people dependent on stimulants, who had never been dependent on drugs or alcohol themselves (apart from nicotine), shared some of the same brain differences from unrelated volunteers. That suggests some differences run in families and may come before drug use, although nobody was scanned before they started using. More of the brothers and sisters than of the volunteers smoked, and the check that smoking did not explain the differences covered only part of the scans. The study shows pictures of brain areas where differences were larger the longer people had used, but gives no numbers and did not separate years of use from age or from other drugs. A review reports other differences found only in the dependent person, but neither the study's report nor its supplement names them. Almost all the dependent people (94 in 100) were dependent on cocaine; the rest were dependent on amphetamines, and the study does not mention meth.
set.magnitude: No cluster statistics in the main report. Supplement, Table S2 (means over voxels selected because they differed between groups, so the differences are inflated): fractional anisotropy 0.55 in controls, 0.53 in non-dependent siblings and 0.52 in dependent siblings (SD 0.02); grey matter in the shared clusters, controls against non-dependent and dependent siblings: left amygdala 0.76 against 0.81 and 0.83, left putamen 0.34 against 0.38 and 0.38, left postcentral gyrus 0.89 against 0.75 and 0.74 (editors' calculation: standardized differences of about 0.7 to 1.3). Fractional anisotropy group difference F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001 (main report; 145 participants with white-matter data, so the degrees of freedom fit one covariate, sex; editors' calculation: η² about 0.27, inflated by the voxel selection). Within-family similarity (one-tailed permutation tests, uncorrected for multiple testing): white matter P = 0.004, putamen P = 0.013, posterior insula P = 0.012, amygdala P = 0.144 (not familial).
set.population: Sibling pairs discordant for stimulant dependence (94% cocaine and 6% amphetamine dependence; UK)
set.comparator: Biological full siblings with no personal history of substance dependence other than nicotine (the supplement's enrolment criterion; the main report says no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse); unrelated controls without a personal or family history of drug or alcohol dependence, similar in age and verbal IQ
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card, no longer provisional now that the supplement has been read: smoking was far more common in the non-dependent siblings than in the controls (55% against 12%) and was checked only for grey matter, by a re-analysis of non-smokers without statistics; the sexes were unbalanced (51% and 64% men; 92% among the dependent siblings), handled by a covariate in the behavioural analyses and by single-sex grey-matter analyses without statistics; and only the clusters shared by both sibling groups are described, with imaging values from voxels selected because they differed.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: 94% of the dependent siblings were dependent on cocaine and 6% (about 3 of 50, editors' calculation) on amphetamines, not further named; no participant is said to have used methamphetamine.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: 50 people per group (146 in the grey-matter and 145 in the white-matter analyses); a grey-matter threshold allowing about one false-positive cluster per map; one-tailed familiality tests without correction for multiple testing.
set.grade.reasoning: One cross-sectional study of 50 sibling pairs, read in full with its supplement. Starts low (observational). Risk of bias, one level: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card: smoking was far more common in the non-dependent siblings than in the controls (55% against 12%) and was checked only for grey matter, by a re-analysis of non-smokers without statistics; the sexes were unbalanced, handled by a covariate in the behavioural analyses and by single-sex grey-matter analyses without statistics; and only the clusters shared by both sibling groups are described, with imaging values from voxels selected because they differed. Indirectness, one level: 94% of the dependent siblings were dependent on cocaine and 6% on amphetamines, and methamphetamine is not mentioned. Imprecision, one level: 50 people per group (146 and 145 in the imaging analyses); grey-matter maps thresholded to allow about one false-positive cluster per map, the shared clusters coming from two comparisons with the same control group; familiality tests one-tailed and not corrected for multiple testing (three of the six would not pass a Bonferroni threshold, editors' calculation). Certainty very low. The claim is rated as an association; whether the shared differences predate use cannot be settled by this design, and the correlations with years of use are shown only as maps, without statistics or adjustment for age.

evidence_set: 50 sibling pairs, one sibling with DSM-IV stimulant dependence and the other with no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse, against 50 unrelated volunteers matched for age and IQ. Both siblings had lower white-matter fractional anisotropy than the volunteers (tract skeleton, F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001), and it was more alike within true sibling pairs than within random pairs (permutation P = 0.004). Three grey-matter clusters were shared by both sibling groups: a larger left amygdala and left putamen, and a smaller left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula; the putamen (P = 0.013) and posterior insula (P = 0.012) differences were familial by the permutation test, the amygdala difference was not (P = 0.144). The main report names no hippocampal, orbitofrontal or anterior insular difference, reports no direct comparison of the two siblings and does not say which stimulants were used.

evidence_add.extracted: Recruited through advertisements and treatment services in East Anglia, UK; all assessed with the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV. Sibling pairs had the same biological parents; one met DSM-IV-TR criteria for cocaine or amphetamine dependence and the other had no personal history of substance dependence except nicotine; controls had no personal or family history of drug or alcohol dependence; all were aged 18–55. Of 154 enrolled, 150 completed (three groups of 50); MRI scans were unavailable for three dependent participants and one sibling, leaving 47, 49 and 50. All dependent participants met DSM-IV-TR criteria for stimulant dependence, 94% for cocaine and 6% for amphetamines (which amphetamines is not stated; methamphetamine is not mentioned); they had used stimulants for a mean of 16.3 years (SD 7.6) from a mean age of 16.5 (SD 2.8); urine was positive for stimulants in all but three; most also met criteria for dependence on another substance (opiates 55%, alcohol 26%, cannabis 9%). Siblings and controls had very low drug and alcohol screening scores and drug-negative urine.

evidence_add.extracted: Table S1 (50 controls, 49 non-dependent siblings, 47 dependent siblings): men 64%, 51% and 92% (chi-square 19.0, P < 0.001); age 32.8, 32.6 and 34.5 years (P = 0.702); verbal IQ 112.3, 108.9 and 110.3 (P = 0.143); education 12.6, 12.1 and 11.6 years (P = 0.062); current smokers 12%, 55% and 94% (chi-square 71.8); upbringing shared until age 10 for 90% and 92% of the two sibling groups and until 15 for 75% and 89%; AUDIT 3.3, 3.9 and 11.4; DAST-20 0.0 and 0.5 in controls and non-dependent siblings. Alcohol use did not differ between non-dependent siblings and controls (t(70.9) = −0.72, P = 0.472). Sex was a covariate in the analyses of demographic and stop-signal data. The dependent participants were tested while still using stimulants, not asked to abstain and screened only for intoxication severe enough to incapacitate them; alcohol was not breathalysed.

evidence_add.page: pp. 4–5, 9 of the Supporting Online Material
evidence_add.locator: Supporting Online Material › Materials and Methods › MRI data processing and analyses (p. 4); DTI data processing and analyses, 1st paragraph (p. 4, continuing on p. 5) and 2nd paragraph (p. 5); Table S2 (p. 9)
evidence_add.extracted: Grey matter was analysed in 50 controls, 47 dependent participants and 49 siblings, and FA in 50, 46 and 49 (one dependent participant could not tolerate the full session). Grey-matter maps were compared with the controls by permutation tests at a cluster-level threshold of one expected false-positive cluster per map (cluster-wise P = 9 × 10⁻⁴ for siblings and 8 × 10⁻⁴ for dependent participants), giving four clusters for the siblings and eight for the dependent participants; the voxels in both lay in three regions, and analyses restricted to men or to women did not change the results. FA: voxel-wise permutation tests with threshold-free cluster enhancement and 5000 permutations, corrected at P < 0.05; mean FA in the significant skeleton was then compared in SPSS. Table S2 (means, SD): FA across the 24,934 skeleton voxels that differed between groups 0.55 (0.02) in controls, 0.53 (0.02) in siblings and 0.52 (0.02) in dependent participants; grey matter in the left amygdala cluster (984 mm³) 0.76, 0.81 and 0.83 (0.07), left putamen (560 mm³) 0.34, 0.38 and 0.38 (0.05–0.06), left postcentral gyrus (1,152 mm³) 0.89, 0.75 and 0.74 (0.11–0.12). Editors' calculation: standardized differences from controls about 0.7, 0.7 and 1.2 SD (siblings) and 1.0, 0.8 and 1.3 SD (dependent participants) for the three grey-matter clusters; all inflated, because the values are means over voxels selected for differing.

evidence_add.extracted: Familiality: the variance of within-pair differences was compared with its distribution when each dependent participant was paired at random with an unrelated sibling (100,000 re-pairings), as a one-tailed test; no adjustment for age or sex is described. Smoking: a re-analysis restricted to non-smoking controls and siblings (numbers not given) kept the amygdala, putamen and postcentral differences significant (Fig. S1, no statistics); no smoking analysis is described for white matter or the stop-signal task, although the section heading names white matter; the sentence after the re-analysis says, as printed, that the siblings' differences might instead be due to tobacco, the opposite of the authors' argument. The supplement labels the shared medial temporal cluster amygdala/hippocampus in its text and in Table S3 (peak −22, −6, −16) but amygdala in Table S2 and Fig. S1, and names no orbitofrontal or anterior insular cluster. Duration of use: maps only (Fig. S2): FA regions negatively correlated with years of stimulant use, less extensive than the familial effect, and grey-matter regions negatively correlated with duration, in places different from the shared clusters; no statistics, region names, correction or adjustment for age are given.

The supplement gives the stimulants (94% cocaine and 6% amphetamine dependence; methamphetamine is not mentioned), which replace the review's account; the siblings' enrolment criterion (no substance dependence other than nicotine); the analysed numbers (146 for grey matter, 145 for white matter, so the white-matter degrees of freedom fit 145 participants with sex as a covariate); the sex and smoking imbalances, with the smoking check limited to grey matter; the grey-matter threshold (about one false-positive cluster per map) and one-tailed familiality tests; the dependent siblings' other dependence (opiates 55%, alcohol 26%) and testing while still using; and the correlations with years of use, shown only as maps without statistics, so the statement no longer says they fit an additional effect of use. The review's hippocampal finding may come from the supplement's label amygdala/hippocampus; its orbitofrontal and anterior insular findings cannot be traced to the study.
